theme: The birth; the shepherds; Simeon and Anna; the boy Jesus
readingInstruction: Read Luke 2:1-52. Luke gives the birth of Jesus with historical care and quiet wonder. Notice who hears the news first, and notice the last verse of the chapter.
settingTheScene: Luke sets the birth of Jesus in the larger world: Caesar Augustus, a census, Quirinius governing Syria. The emperor is moving millions of people with a decree, yet the real King is being born in a stable to a peasant couple. Luke wants us to see the contrast between earthly power and heavenly power. Bethlehem is the city of David, so the birth fulfills the promise that the Messiah would come from David’s line.
observation: “And she gave birth to her firstborn son and wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn” (2:7).
“And in the same region there were shepherds out in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night” (2:8).
“Fear not, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people” (2:10).
“For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord” (2:11).
“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased!” (2:14).
“But Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart” (2:19).
“For my eyes have seen your salvation… a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel” (2:30-32).
“And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man” (2:52).
interpretation:
The birth is told simply. There is no room for them in the inn, and the Savior is laid in a feeding trough. The Son of God enters the world in poverty and obscurity.

The first announcement is not to the powerful but to shepherds, who were low on the social ladder and often distrusted. An angel appears, and the glory of the Lord shines around them. The news is “good news of great joy that will be for all the people,” and the titles in verse 11 are rich. The child is a Savior, the Christ, and the Lord. A baby in a manger is all three. The shepherds go in haste, find the child as they were told, and return glorifying and praising God. They are the first evangelists.

When the child is brought to the temple, two old people recognize him. Simeon had been promised by the Spirit that he would not die before seeing the Lord’s Christ. He takes the child in his arms and sings: his eyes have seen salvation, prepared in the presence of all peoples, “a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel.” This is the universal note of Luke. Simeon also tells Mary that a sword will pierce her own soul, because the child will cause the rising and falling of many and be opposed. Joy and sorrow are linked from the start. Anna, an elderly prophetess who never left the temple, gives thanks and tells everyone who was waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.

The chapter ends with the twelve-year-old Jesus in the temple, listening to teachers and asking questions. When his parents find him, he says, “Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house?” Already he knows who his Father is. And yet he goes home and is subject to them. The Son of God grows up, with all the ordinary stages of human life.
connection: Micah 5:2 names Bethlehem as the place of the ruler’s birth. Isaiah 9:6 says to us a child is born. Isaiah 49:6 speaks of a light for the nations. Luke 2:34-35 points ahead to the cross. Philippians 2:6-8 describes the Son who emptied himself and took the form of a servant. 2 Corinthians 8:9 says that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor. Hebrews 2:14 says he shared in our flesh and blood.
application:
Take time to listen to the angels’ words as if they were spoken to you: “Fear not… unto you is born this day a Savior.”

Ponder, like Mary, one thing from this week’s reading. Hold it in your heart and pray over it.

Be like the shepherds and tell someone the good news of great joy this week.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for sending his Son in humility.
Tell him what it is like to hear that the news of his birth is for all people.
Ask him to teach you to treasure it, as Mary did.
